--- Page 1 ---
PEAK-MEMORY SCHEDULES YOU CAN TRUST: EXACT REALIZATION,
CERTIFIED OPTIMALITY, AND THE LIMITS OF RECOMPUTATION FOR
INFERENCE
Ivan Fomin 1 Ivan Koryabkin 1 Boris Sheludko 1
ABSTRACT
Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator
order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order,
handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program
misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in
19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program,
build an exact model of its memory behaviour from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute
those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It
does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in every one of our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize
why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse “trap” lower
bounds, each computable with O(n2) minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out
wrapper graphs and for all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. The certificates show that
most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering
is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified
optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even
at treewidth two, it encodes knapsack exactly on series–parallel graphs, and it is solvable exactly on bounded
treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap
value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers
the peak by 5.2–6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
1
INTRODUCTION
A neural network that runs in real time on a phone, a hear-
ing aid or a microcontroller has to fit its activations into a
fixed, small memory budget, and it has to do so without
slowing down. Most of the familiar levers for reducing
activation memory trade it for time. Rematerialization re-
computes values instead of storing them (Chen et al., 2016;
Jain et al., 2020). Offloading moves them to slower memory.
Patch-based execution recomputes overlapping receptive
fields (Lin et al., 2021). For training these trades are usu-
ally acceptable, because a few percent of throughput buys
a larger batch. For real-time inference they often are not:
a keyword spotter or a streaming speech model has a hard
deadline per frame. The interesting levers there are the ones
that are free in time, such as the order in which operators
1Yandex, Moscow, Russia.

run, and the recomputations that cost very little time but
remove a large buffer.
Operator order is already exploited.
PyTorch Inductor
ships a peak-memory reordering pass that is enabled by
default (Ansel et al., 2024). TensorFlow Lite Micro plans
a static arena for the order it is given (David et al., 2021).
A line of work schedules irregular graphs exactly or hierar-
chically (Ahn et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Steiner et al.,
2023; Jin et al., 2023). These systems share an implicit as-
sumption: if a better order is found on the compiler’s graph,
the deployed program will be better by the predicted amount.
They also leave a practical question unanswered, namely
when to stop. A deployment engineer who has run a sched-
uler cannot tell whether the result is optimal or whether a
better order exists that the heuristic missed.
This paper makes peak-memory scheduling trustworthy in
both senses. We show that the assumption above is false in
a mainstream compiler, give a realization method for which
it is true by construction, and give certificates that settle
the question of when to stop. We then ask what selective
arXiv:2610.23328v1  [cs.LG]  16 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
recomputation can add once the order is exhausted. The
answer is a mix of good and bad news that we think is useful
to state precisely.
Regeneration is unreliable.
The usual way to deploy a
better order is to hand it back to the compiler and regen-
erate code. Code generation, however, runs after schedul-
ing. It decides how kernels are grouped into calls, which
dead buffers are reused in place, and when references are
dropped, and a new order changes those decisions. Across
54 compiled CPU configurations of 16 architectures, the
regenerated program misses its own predicted peak in 22
cases and is worse than the stock program in 9. On a GPU
it is worse than stock in 19 of 50 configurations and, in
addition, changes numerical results (Section 5.1).
Fixed-wrapper realization is exact.
We instead take the
generated program as it is, profile one execution, and build
an exact model of its memory behaviour at the granularity
of its statements. We then permute the program’s own state-
ments. Kernels, arguments and buffer reuse stay untouched;
only the order and the placement of allocations and releases
change. Under an explicit contract the realized peak equals
the modeled peak (Theorem 1). On CPU this holds to the
byte in all 78 training runs and all 22 inference runs, and
outputs and gradients are bitwise identical to the stock pro-
gram. On a GPU the CUDA caching allocator violates one
condition of the contract, and we characterize exactly how
(Section 5.6).
Certificates tell us when to stop.
We give two lower
bounds on the optimal peak, a forward and a reverse “trap”
bound. Each is computable with O(n2) minimum cuts, and
each dominates the classical event-cut bound. Together
they prove the found order optimal for 115 of 122 held-
out wrapper graphs, in well under a second, and for all
16 microcontroller-class models we study. This changes
the practical conversation. For most inference graphs the
certificate shows that the stock order is already optimal, so
no scheduler can help. The exception is branching networks,
where reordering is free and the saving can be large: 10.0%
on DeepLabV3 inference.
The limits of recomputation.
When the certified opti-
mum is still above the budget, recomputation is the next
lever, and for inference it is attractive only if it is selec-
tive, recomputing a few cheap values rather than whole
subgraphs. We model this with per-operator recomputation
caps kv, as in Moccasin (Bartan et al., 2023), and prove
three things.
• Peak feasibility is strongly NP-hard for every fixed uni-
form cap, already at treewidth two.
• Minimizing extra work under cap two is exactly a knap-
sack problem on series–parallel graphs.
• An exact algorithm exists on bounded treewidth, but with
a necessary dependence on the numeric budget.
Empirically, recomputation at tensor granularity cannot help
the public tiny models we study. In every one of them the
peak is set by a single operator’s inputs and output, a bound
no schedule of whole tensors can beat (Section 5.2). Recom-
putation pays off where a large value is held across the net-
work only for a late reuse and can be recreated cheaply from
a small ancestor. The public ReDimNet speaker-embedding
networks have exactly this structure. In all seven sizes their
order is already optimal, yet recomputing the stem once
lowers the peak by 5.2–6.1% at no more than 0.34% extra
MACs (Section 5.3). For such values our model of caps
and our certificates apply directly; for tiny models whose
peak is a single layer, savings require splitting tensors, as
patch-based inference does (Lin et al., 2021).
We do not propose a new search heuristic; the search in
our pipeline is an existing exact capacity search. Our con-
tributions are the realization method, the certificates, the
measurements that show where scheduling can and can-
not help, and the complexity results that delimit selective
recomputation.
2
BACKGROUND AND MODEL
The one-shot root model.
A schedule executes each oper-
ation of a directed acyclic graph once. Operation v allocates
new buffers (“roots”) of total size a(v) and may use tran-
sient memory, and both are allocated before any of its inputs
can be released. A root is live after a set S of executed
operations if it has been produced and is either pinned (it
outlives the program, like a returned output) or still has an
unexecuted consumer. Writing L(S) for the live bytes and
s(v) ≥0 for the transient envelope of v, executing v after S
costs L(S)+a(v)+s(v). The peak of an order is its largest
event cost, and OPT is the smallest peak over topological
orders. Multi-output calls, views and external inputs are ex-
pressed by roots with several consumers. L is submodular
on the lattice of ideals, which is what makes minimum-cut
arguments work below.
Compiled programs.
PyTorch Inductor lowers a model
to a flat Python wrapper that allocates buffers, calls gen-
erated C++ or Triton kernels and library kernels (matrix
multiplication, convolution, attention), aliases dead buffers
for reuse, and drops references with del. For training,
AOTAutograd produces one wrapper for the forward and
one for the backward pass. The point that matters for this
paper is that storage is born and freed by the wrapper, not
by the graph the scheduler sees. Deployment runtimes for
microcontrollers, such as TFLite Micro, instead execute op-
erators in model order and place every tensor in a statically


--- Page 3 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
planned arena (David et al., 2021). On GPUs, PyTorch uses
a caching allocator that rounds requests and reuses cached
blocks. Section 5.6 shows that this difference between static,
exact allocation and history-dependent caching is decisive
for whether a modeled peak is realized.
3
REALIZING A SCHEDULE EXACTLY
Figure 1 summarizes the method. We compile the model
once with the stock compiler and capture every generated
wrapper. We then run one warm step in which each wrapper
statement executes inside a profiler scope. After each state-
ment we record the storage address and size bound to every
name it assigns. Every allocation and free event is thereby
attributed to a statement. Storages are identified by allo-
cation epoch rather than by address, because the allocator
reuses addresses.
From statements to a root model.
Each statement that
calls a kernel or a library function becomes a unit. A state-
ment that only allocates a buffer joins the first unit that
touches that buffer, so allocation happens as late as possible.
Aliases (views, tuple projections and the reuse assignments
Inductor emits) and del statements are not units; they are
placed during emission. A storage that is allocated and freed
inside a single statement is a transient and contributes to
that unit’s envelope s(v). Every other storage born in the
program becomes a root produced by its unit. Its consumers
are the units that touch any name bound to it, and it is pinned
if it outlives the call. Because a profiled storage is identified
with all the names that ever referred to it, ownership through
views and tuples is accounted for exactly.
Dependencies from read/write effects.
Ordering con-
straints come from data flow at storage level. For generated
C++ kernels we read the const-ness of every pointer parame-
ter from the emitted signature. For Triton kernels we use the
role encoded in the parameter name (in ptr, out ptr,
in out ptr). For library calls, the out= argument and
the first argument of a mutating operator are writes. Calls
we do not recognize are serialized with every other unit. Per
storage we then add read-after-write, write-after-read and
write-after-write edges, which leaves readers of the same
buffer generation free to reorder. This distinction turns out
to matter more than the search itself (Section 5.4).
Emission.
Given a unit order, we emit the original state-
ments, each exactly once. Allocations go immediately be-
fore their unit, and aliases, assertions and dels go as early
as their dependencies allow. No statement is synthesized
and no release is invented. The one exception is renaming:
a few generated wrappers rebind an input name, and we re-
name it so that every name is assigned once, deleting the old
binding where the original rebinding would have dropped it.
The reordered function is compiled into the same module,
so it calls the very kernel objects that were profiled.
Theorem 1 (Exact realization). Assume the generated pro-
gram satisfies a contract with six conditions: (C1) region-
level effects are complete; (C2) ownership and completion
are as recorded; (C3) each unit computes a deterministic
function of its inputs; (C4) each unit’s sequence of alloca-
tion events is as recorded; (C5) that sequence is indepen-
dent of the surrounding live memory (the frame condition);
(C6) emission introduces no other events. Then every unit or-
der that respects the dependencies preserves the program’s
results, bitwise if the kernels are deterministic, and realizes
exactly the peak predicted by the root model.
The proof (Section C) is an event-by-event simulation that
maintains a correspondence between modeled and concrete
live storage, owners and buffer generations. Its ingredients
are standard. Staged effects exist in MLIR (LLVM Project,
2026), and heap simulation over an instruction sequence
exists in XLA (OpenXLA, 2026). What is specific is that
the composition survives direct permutation of a generated
program that calls opaque library kernels. The contract is
not proven for library kernels, so our harness never trusts it.
Every emitted program is re-profiled, and the measured peak
of every wrapper is compared with the prediction. During
development this check caught two bugs of our own. An
alias used only by the final return was emitted too late, and it
kept a tuple, and with it a 16 KB gradient, alive. Stochastic-
depth layers in some vision models made even the stock
program non-reproducible. Both were fixed before the runs
reported here.
Search.
The root models have up to 259 units. We search
with an exact capacity search: depth-first search over ideals
with forced non-increasing steps and minimum-cut packet
closure. It bisects the capacity between the lower bound
of Section 4 and the peak of the stock order. In almost all
graphs it reaches the certified bound within milliseconds, so
the search is not where the difficulty lies.

4
CERTIFYING THAT NO BETTER ORDER
EXISTS
A scheduler that returns a peak U is only half an answer;
the other half is a lower bound LB with LB = U, which
proves that no order is better. For an operation v let A(v)
be its strict ancestors and D(v) its descendants including v.
The classical event-cut bound asks, for every v, how small
the live memory can possibly be just before v runs:
G = max
v
h
a(v) + s(v) +
min
X ideal: A(v)⊆X, v /∈X L(X)
i
.
Each inner minimum is a minimum-weight closure, i.e. one
minimum cut. The bound can be loose because the cheap-
est prefix for one operation may be incompatible with the
cheapest prefix for another.
Definition 2 (Trap bounds). Let c(v) = a(v) + s(v). For
a proper ideal R with ready frontier F(R), let fv(R) =
c(v) + min{L(X) : A(v) ⊆X
⊆R} and F
=
maxR minv∈F (R) fv(R). For a nonempty ideal T and max-
imal v ∈T, let qv(T) = c(v) + min{L(X) : T \ {v} ⊆
X ⊆V \ D(v)} and R = maxT minv qv(T).
The forward bound F rests on a simple observation. Every
order leaves any proper ideal R through some first opera-
tion, and at that moment its actual prefix lies between that
operation’s ancestors and R. The reverse bound R uses the
last operation of any nonempty ideal T instead. Neither
argument assumes that the minimizing prefix is reachable,
which is why both are sound but can be loose.
Theorem 3. (a) G ≤F ≤OPT and G ≤R ≤OPT.
(b) Each of F and R can be computed with O(n2) minimum-
cut calls, independently of the magnitude of the weights.
(c) The two bounds are incomparable. (d) OPT/F is un-
bounded even on binary in-trees and on a family of pairwise
merges, while R = OPT on both families.
Domination holds because the ideal V \ D(v) has v as its
only ready operation, which reproduces the event-cut term
for v. Computation uses monotone optimistic saturation.
For F, we repeatedly admit a frontier operation of smallest
fv(R) and record the running maximum; the reverse bound
removes maximal operations symmetrically. Proofs, both
strict separations and the two families appear in Section D.
A certificate consists of the stuck ideal and one flow/cut
pair per frontier operation. Our verifier recomputes liveness
from the graph, checks every cut value against its flow and
replays the upper order, without importing the solver or
running max-flow.
Whether OPT/ max(F, R) is bounded is open. Figure 2a
shows how tight the bounds are in practice. On 800 random
DAGs of up to 14 vertices (series–parallel, pumpkin, tree,
random and training-shaped), compared against the exact
optimum, max(F, R) is exact in 773 cases. The event-cut
bound G is exact in only 671. The reverse bound is the
stronger of the two: it beats F in 98 instances and loses in
11. The worst ratio we found is 1.23 on random graphs and
1.50 with an adversarial hill-climb over 13-vertex graphs.

5
EVALUATION
Setup.
All runs use PyTorch 2.14.1 with Inductor. On
CPU, every run uses FP32 and one thread; we also re-
peat the inference grid in bfloat16.
The GPU is an
NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti with a CUDA 12.6 build of
the same release.
The stock baseline is Inductor with
reorder for peak memory and in-place buffer reuse
enabled; only the compile cache is disabled. Dropout and
stochastic depth are disabled. Weights are random unless
stated otherwise; Section 5.7 shows that pretrained weights
give identical schedules and peaks. Inference runs evaluate
the model in evaluation mode without gradients. Train-
ing runs measure one compiled forward pass, an MSE loss
against a fixed random target and the backward pass, with-
out an optimizer step. Peak is the maximum of tracked
tensor allocations inside the measured step; it excludes the
resident weights and inputs, which we add back where we
report savings “including the frame”. Every run measures
the stock, the normalized (our emission of the stock unit or-
der) and the reordered program twice, and compares outputs
and all gradients bitwise across them.
The study has four parts:
• server-scale inference: 22 configurations, including seg-
mentation networks, CNNs, and Transformer prefill with
long sequences;
• microcontroller-class inference: 16 models, among them
the four MLPerf Tiny reference networks (Banbury et al.,
2021; Zhang et al., 2017), TC-ResNet keyword spot-
ters (Choi et al., 2019), small MobileNets, MNASNet,
ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet, EfficientNet-B0, GoogLeNet
and a tiny U-Net;
• compiled training: 50 configurations of 16 architectures,
plus shape sweeps, ablations and seed repeats;
• the GPU replication.
5.1
Regeneration is unreliable
For every configuration we also map the optimized unit
order back to Inductor’s scheduler nodes, force it in the
reordering pass, recompile, and measure. Figure 3 plots the
outcome against the saving that fixed-wrapper realization
achieves with the same order. If regeneration were faithful,
all points would lie on the diagonal. On CPU the regener-
ated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 training
configurations. Where a saving exists it realizes 0.94% on
average instead of 1.97%. In 9 configurations it is worse
than stock, once by 30.6% (T5 encoder at sequence length
512). On the GPU the picture is worse: regeneration is
worse than stock in 19 of 50 configurations. The post-fusion
graph is unchanged in all of these cases. What changes is
how kernels are grouped into calls and which dead buffers
are reused; for the encoder–decoder, 559 backward state-
ments become 554. Since recompiled kernels also round
differently, regeneration on GPU additionally changes gra-
dients, while fixed-wrapper realization does not. A memory
scheduler that may silently make a program worse, and
change its numerics, is hard to deploy; this is the main
reason we realize schedules on the generated program.
5.2
Inference: where reordering helps and where it
cannot
For server-scale inference, fixed-wrapper realization is ex-
act in all 22 configurations, with zero prediction error and
bitwise-identical outputs. The saving, however, is concen-
trated.
Only one configuration improves: DeepLabV3-
ResNet50 at 512 × 512, whose peak drops by 10.0%.
DeepLabV3’s atrous spatial pyramid has five parallel
branches over a large feature map, and the stock order keeps
several of their outputs alive at once. In the other configu-
rations the certificates prove the stock order optimal for 20

in Section 5.5. This includes ResNet, MobileNetV2, Effi-
cientNet, DenseNet, Inception, Swin, ViT, BERT, GPT-2
and Llama prefill at up to 2048 tokens. Inference graphs are
mostly chains of blocks whose activations die immediately,
so a single sensible order is all there is. The practical value
of the certificate is precisely to say so, and to direct effort
elsewhere.
Public microcontroller-class models.
For the tiny mod-
els we build the operator graph the way an embedded run-
time sees it. Batch normalization is folded into convolutions,
activations are fused into their producer, views are aliases,
and activations are int8. We compare the order in which
TFLite Micro would execute the model with the certified
optimum, and evaluate the arena with a TFLite-Micro-style
greedy planner. The certificates prove the model order al-
ready optimal for all 16 models (up to 134 operators), and
executing every schedule reproduces the modeled peak ex-
actly. More importantly, in every one of them the peak
equals a trivial lower bound: the inputs plus the output of a
single operator. Figure 4 shows why. The memory profile of
a tiny CNN has a sharp early spike at a high-resolution layer
(MobileNets), or one at a skip-concatenation (U-Net), and
the rest of the network is far below it. No schedule of whole
tensors, with or without recomputation, can go below that
single-operator bound. The capped-recomputation solver,
given a cap of two on every operator, accordingly never
finds a feasible reduction. These models are deliberately de-
signed so that the early high-resolution layer dominates, and
further savings for them require splitting that layer’s tensors
into tiles, as patch-based inference does (Lin et al., 2021;

Alwani et al., 2016). Tiling recomputes the halo regions
between tiles, which is exactly the selective recomputation
with per-vertex caps studied in Section 6, now on a tile-level
graph.
5.3
Selective recomputation on a speaker-embedding
network
ReDimNet (Yakovlev et al., 2024) is a family of speaker-
embedding networks designed for on-device speaker recog-
nition, in seven sizes (B0–B6). We take the public Vox-
Celeb2 checkpoints and trace each backbone at the operator
level, fusing normalization and activations into their produc-
ers, with fp32 activations. Inputs are 2 s and 0.8 s of audio
(201 and 81 feature frames); the latter is the typical window
of a streaming engine. At every stage ReDimNet aggregates
the outputs of all previous stages, and every stage also reads
the stem output again. The stem output is therefore held
across the whole network for these late reuses, although it is
a short and cheap function of the input features, which are
small.
For every model the certificates prove the model order al-
ready optimal, so reordering alone gains nothing. We then
keep the small input features alive and recompute the stem
chain once from them for its late uses. The transformed
graph is rescheduled exactly, and the certificates prove the
new order optimal for it as well. Executing the resulting
schedule reproduces the modeled peak, and the output is
bitwise identical to the original model. Table 1 shows the
2 s results; the 0.8 s results have the same relative savings.
The peak falls by 5.2–6.1% at 0.02–0.34% extra MACs,
the smaller models paying more because their stem is a

larger share of the work. For B3 and B6 a greedy arena
planner loses the saving to fragmentation; a joint order-and-
placement step would be needed there. Recomputing the
stage outputs themselves would not help, because each of
them is a direct input of every later aggregation, including
the one at the peak. The pattern that rewards selective re-
computation is a value held only for a late reuse that does
not coincide with the peak event.
On internal production on-device models, which we cannot
release, the same selective recomputation reduced the de-
ployed TFLite activation arena by up to 15% at about 1%
extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs. These numbers
are reported for context only; all claims in this paper rest on
the public models above.
5.4
Compiled training
Training graphs have more freedom, because the backward
pass interleaves gradient computation with the release of
saved activations. Table 2 summarizes the savings of fixed-
wrapper realization on CPU, and Table 4 in Section B.1 lists
every configuration.
The saving comes from lifetimes at the critical backward
call, not from allocation volume, which is identical in both
programs. Figure 5 shows the backward wrapper of a two-
layer Transformer encoder. The stock order materializes
two parameter gradients, of 64 KiB and 16 KiB, before the
flash-attention backward call. The reordered program defers
them past that call, holding one 32 KiB activation a little
longer in exchange. The net saving is 48 KiB, and the new
peak equals the certified lower bound. CNNs gain only

Figure 5. Live memory at each unit of the backward wrapper of a

where the backward pass has parallel branches (ResNet-
50, ConvNeXt, Swin); chain-like ones are already optimal,
and their certificates prove it. The savings do not follow a
simple rule. Over the batch and sequence sweeps they are
non-monotone, because the critical call changes with the
shape. Section B.6 gives two families in which either of the
obvious rules, “finish the gradient branch first” or “always
defer gradients”, nearly doubles the peak.
Precise effects matter more than search.
If every storage
access is treated as a write, as a conservative implementa-
tion might do, most of the saving disappears. The encoder
loses all of its 4.6%, the large-sequence encoder all of its
4.7%, and DistilBERT all of its 2.3%; the encoder–decoder
drops from 7.6% to 6.2%. The freedom lies in reordering
readers of the same buffer generation, for example the two
matrix multiplications of a linear layer’s backward pass.
Disabling Inductor’s own memory pass leaves the stock
peak unchanged in six of eight configurations, and raises
it by 1.3% and 1.9% in the other two. From either start-
ing point, fixed-wrapper realization ends below the stock
program with the pass enabled.
5.5
Certificates on held-out models
None of the models in this section were used to design the
bounds. On the 122 forward and backward wrapper graphs
of the training grid and the inference grid, the trap bounds
certify the found order optimal in 115 cases (94%). The
forward bound alone certifies 99 and the reverse bound alone
112, as Figure 2a shows. In training the remaining gaps,
between 0.36% and 1.50%, occur in the backward graphs of
DistilBERT, BERT and ViT-B. In inference there is a single
open case, RegNetY-400MF, with a gap of 13%, the only
graph where the bounds are clearly loose. These gaps may
be due either to the bound or to the search. As a baseline
we posed the same infeasibility question (OPT −1) to CP-


--- Page 8 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
SAT with an exact cumulative model (Figure 2b). CP-SAT
answers 91 of 94 queries, with a median time of 0.02 s and a
maximum of 66 s, and times out on 3. The certificates need
a median of 0.004 s and at most 0.25 s, and unlike CP-SAT
they can be checked independently.
5.6
GPU replication and the caching allocator
We reran the training grid and the sweeps on the GPU (50
configurations). The wrappers there call Triton kernels.
Correctness carries over. In all 27 configurations where the
stock program is itself deterministic, the reordered program
is bitwise identical. In the other 23, where cuDNN or the
attention backward use atomics, the reordered gradients
differ from stock by no more than stock differs from itself.
Exactness does not carry over (Figure 6). Fixed-wrapper
realization lowers the peak reported by the allocator in 25
configurations, by a median of 1.3% and up to 7.4%, but it
raises it in 8, by up to 1.5%. The block-level prediction is
exact in only 17 of 49.
The cause is the frame condition (C5) of Theorem 1. The
CUDA caching allocator rounds requests, and in its large-
block pool it does not split off remainders below 1 MiB.
Which block a tensor receives, and therefore how many
bytes it occupies, depends on the allocation history. The log-
ical peak, measured by the allocator’s requested bytes
counter, moves exactly as on CPU; the 8-layer Llama, for
example, drops by 0.86% in both settings. Expandable
segments do not remove the effect. Replaying the CPU
traces through a model of the caching allocator tells the
same story. Of the 24 configurations with a logical saving,
reserved memory decreases in 6, stays the same in 13 be-
cause 20 MiB segments absorb the change, and increases in
5. Because a single profiled step measures the true peak, we
deploy reorderings on GPU behind a guard that keeps the
stock program unless the measured peak improves. With
the guard no configuration regresses, and the mean saving is
0.92%. Static arenas, which embedded runtimes and ahead-
of-time compilers use, do not have this problem. There
the allocation is a function of the schedule alone, so the
condition holds by construction.
5.7
Precision, pretrained weights and cost
In bfloat16 inference (6 configurations) fixed-wrapper re-
alization is again exact and bitwise identical to stock in 6
cases, and the certificates again prove the stock order op-
timal. The schedule depends only on shapes and on the
generated program, not on weight values. With pretrained
torchvision and Hugging Face checkpoints (6 configura-
tions), the stock and optimized peaks are identical to those
with random weights in 6 cases, and realization is exact
in 6. In particular, pretrained DeepLabV3 saves the same
10.0%. One caveat concerns DeepLabV3’s default torchvi-

sion checkpoint, which adds an auxiliary FCN head. That

by 10% and makes the stock order optimal. Saving mem-

needed. Reordering does not change the step time. In an
alternating protocol over 10 CPU configurations, the median
reordered-to-stock time ratio is 0.997, within [0.959, 1.045].
On GPU the median ratio is 0.998. Profiling, building the
model and certification take one extra step plus under a
second for almost every graph.
6
SELECTIVE RECOMPUTATION AND ITS
LIMITS
When the certified optimum is still above the memory bud-
get, the remaining lever is recomputation. For real-time
inference it is acceptable only in a selective form, where a
few cheap values are recomputed so that a large buffer need
not be kept. We model this as in Moccasin (Bartan et al.,
2023). Vertex v produces an immutable value of wv bytes at
price cv (for example its MACs), and it may be computed at
most kv times. Its inputs must be resident when it runs, and
its output is allocated before inputs are released. The ques-
tion is how little extra work buys a given memory budget B.
Uniform caps kv = k and individual caps express different
policies. An individual cap of two on cheap elementwise
operators and one everywhere else is the kind of policy a
real-time system can afford.
Certificates of necessary recomputation.
The one-shot
bounds of Section 4 carry over. If a capped schedule com-
puted every vertex of a set P exactly once with peak at
most B, then the order of first computations would be a

one-shot schedule of the graph with all weights outside P
set to zero, with peak at most B (Theorem 8). Hence any
one-shot certificate above B for that projected graph proves
that some vertex of P must be recomputed. Constraints on
individual events strengthen this into a lower bound on the
extra work. Every once-computed value that must survive
an event contributes to that event’s memory, which yields
a knapsack-cover constraint on the recomputed bytes (Sec-
tion E). On 375 small DAGs with uniform cap two, where
we compute everything exactly, three findings stand out.
• Recomputation lowers the optimal peak in 117 of them,
by a mean factor of 0.942.
• Below the one-shot optimum, the projection certificate
proves that recomputation is necessary in 270 of 290
budgets.
• The cover bound explains on average 43% of the exact
extra work.
Complexity.
Table 3 summarizes what can and cannot be
computed efficiently.
Theorem 4. For every fixed k ≥1, deciding whether a
DAG with uniform recomputation cap k can compute its
sink with peak at most B is strongly NP-complete, even on
DAGs of treewidth at most two.
For k = 1 this is the strong NP-hardness of weighted one-
shot scheduling on pumpkin graphs, which have treewidth
two (Jin et al., 2023). For larger k we append a reset gadget:
k phases separated by barriers of weight B, which force
every old value to be evicted. With a uniform cap of k each
old vertex then runs exactly once per phase, so each phase
is a one-shot schedule. The gadget is a fan at the sink and
keeps the treewidth at two (Section F). Small interfaces do
not help either. On series–parallel graphs with out-degree
two and a uniform cap of two, the minimum extra work is
exactly the optimum of a knapsack instance,

An exact algorithm on bounded treewidth.
Theorem 5. Given a tree decomposition of width t and
an integer budget B, the minimum total work subject to
peak at most B and all caps can be computed in time
f(t, K, B)poly(n, L), where K bounds the caps and L is
the input length.
The difficulty is that the obvious interface state, namely
which boundary values are resident and how often each was
computed, is not sufficient. Two histories can agree on it and
still differ in which internal vertices have exhausted their
caps (Section G). The algorithm therefore records, at each
node of the decomposition, the complete word of compute
and delete events of the bag vertices, of length at most
2K(t + 1). Between consecutive boundary events it keeps
the typical-sequence reduction (Bodlaender et al., 2020)
of the private memory profile, of length at most 2B + 1,
together with a literal witness schedule. Theorem 4 shows
that the dependence on B cannot be reduced to poly(B)
unless P=NP. A rounding step yields a schedule with peak
at most (1 + ε)B and work at most that of any schedule
with at most p live values (Section G). The algorithm is
a statement about tractability, not a tool. Our prototype
exceeds 3 · 106 states on width-two graphs with six vertices
at K = 2 and B = 8 (Section B.7).
What this means for tiny models.
On the public
microcontroller-class models of Section 5.2, recomputa-
tion of whole tensors is useless, because the peak is a single
operator’s footprint. Tiling that operator, and possibly its
neighbours, turns one large vertex into many small ones
that share halo regions. Recomputing a halo is then a cap
kv > 1 on a small vertex, and the extra work is the halo’s
MACs. Tile-level graphs of a few early layers are narrow,
so the exact machinery of this section, together with the
certificates of Section 4, applies to them directly. Choos-
ing tile shapes jointly with the schedule, under an explicit
latency budget and with a certificate of optimality, is the
natural continuation of this work. Patch-based inference
today chooses them heuristically (Lin et al., 2021).
7
RELATED WORK
Peak-memory scheduling.
Register sufficiency, the unit-
weight version of the problem, is NP-complete (Sethi, 1975).
Jin et al. prove strong NP-hardness of the weighted one-shot


--- Page 10 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
problem on pumpkins and out-trees, and give exact algo-
rithms for series–parallel graphs based on dominant sched-
ules (Jin et al., 2023). SERENITY schedules irregularly
wired networks for edge devices by dynamic programming
and graph rewriting (Ahn et al., 2020). HMCOS expands
hierarchical groups around the peak (Wang et al., 2022).
MODeL optimizes order and address placement jointly with
an ILP (Steiner et al., 2023), and Zhong et al. fold safe sub-
graphs before solving an ILP (Zhong et al., 2023). Lower
bounds based on event cuts and wavefronts are standard in
I/O complexity (Elango et al., 2014), and iterated optimistic
admission against resource bounds is the LP–RPG pattern
in planning (Coles et al., 2013). Our trap bounds special-
ize these ideas to tensor roots. To our knowledge, their
domination over the event-cut bound, their incomparability
and their computation with O(n2) cuts have not been stated
before.
Memory planning in compilers and embedded runtimes.
XLA’s heap simulator accounts for allocation, free and shar-
ing events over an instruction sequence (OpenXLA, 2026).
MLIR provides staged side effects and ownership-based
deallocation (LLVM Project, 2026). Exo verifies schedules
of low-level code against memory effects (Ikarashi et al.,
2022). µ-TWO profiles memory and executes optimized
schedules for multi-model training (Purandare et al., 2023).
TFLite Micro executes operators in model order over a
statically planned arena (David et al., 2021). MCUNet co-
designs architectures and inference for microcontrollers (Lin
et al., 2020), and MCUNetV2 executes early layers patch
by patch, recomputing overlaps (Lin et al., 2021), as fused-
layer accelerators do in hardware (Alwani et al., 2016). Sun
et al. study recomputation for peak-memory reduction of
inference on IoT devices (Sun et al., 2023). Our contribu-
tions are the measurement that regeneration is unreliable,
a realization that is exact on the generated program, and
certificates that say when scheduling is finished.
Rematerialization.
Checkpointing for chains goes back
to revolve (Griewank & Walther, 2000) and to sublinear-
memory training (Chen et al., 2016). Heterogeneous chains
admit optimal dynamic programs (Herrmann et al., 2019).
Checkmate (Jain et al., 2020), Moccasin (Bartan et al.,
2023), Rockmate (Zhao et al., 2023), HiRemate (Gusak
et al., 2025), MAGIS (Chen et al., 2024) and DTR (Kirisame
et al., 2021) optimize recomputation with MILP, con-
straint programming, hierarchy, graph transformations or
online policies. Kumar et al. bound recomputation through
treewidth (Kumar et al., 2019). Bounded-width composi-
tion and typical sequences are classical (Downey & Fellows,
1999; Bodlaender & Kloks, 1996; Bodlaender et al., 2020),
and unrestricted pebbling is PSPACE-complete (Gilbert
et al., 1980; Chan et al., 2023). Our complexity results
delimit what selective recomputation with caps can achieve,
which is the form relevant to real-time inference.
8
LIMITATIONS
Exactness, as stated in Theorem 1, holds for allocators that
return exactly what is requested, which is the case on our
CPU runs and in static arenas. For the CUDA caching allo-
cator we fall back to a measured guard. Searching against a
simulated caching allocator could restore exactness, since
its behaviour is deterministic for a fixed single-stream re-
quest sequence, but we have not yet matched the simula-
tor to the device, whose initial state includes the segments
holding parameters. Library kernels’ effects and alloca-
tion sequences are profiled and checked by re-measurement,
not proven, and every model is specific to one input shape.
The tiny-model study evaluates the operator graph and a
greedy arena planner, not firmware on a microcontroller.
The savings from reordering are small except on branching
networks, typically 1–3% in training and zero on most infer-
ence graphs. We present this as a finding that the certificates
make visible, not as a weakness of the search. Theorem 5 is
impractical, its novelty relative to general finite-state peb-
bling frameworks was checked only by a bounded literature
review, and whether OPT/ max(F, R) is bounded remains
open.
9
CONCLUSION
For memory-constrained inference, the cheapest memory is
the memory saved by a free schedule change, and the most
useful answer a scheduler can give is a certified one. We
showed that a schedule must be realized on the program that
runs: regenerating code for a better order is unreliable, while
permuting the generated program under a checked contract
is exact. Polynomial-time certificates show that most infer-
ence graphs, and all the public microcontroller-class models
we studied, are already scheduled optimally, and they iden-
tify the branching networks where reordering pays. Beyond
the certified optimum, selective recomputation with caps is
computationally hard in every general sense we examined.
It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single
layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late
reuse it pays: 5.2–6.1% on ReDimNet at under 0.4% extra
MACs. This points to certified tile-level schedules as the
way to buy memory at a bounded, explicit cost in latency.

APPENDIX OVERVIEW
The appendix is organized in four parts. Section A describes the experimental setup in enough detail to reproduce every
number in the paper. Section B reports the complete results behind the summaries of Section 5, including the configurations
that appear only in aggregate in the main text. Sections C to G contain the proofs, in the order in which the results appear in
the paper. Section H describes the supplementary archive.
A
EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
A.1
Software and hardware
All CPU experiments use PyTorch 2.14.1 (CPU build), Hugging Face Transformers 4.57.1 and torchvision 0.29.1 on a single
thread (OMP NUM THREADS=1) of a 22-core x86-64 workstation. GPU experiments use the CUDA 12.6 build of the same
PyTorch release on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti (Turing, 11 GB), one GPU per configuration, with no other process
on the device. CP-SAT is the OR-Tools implementation with one worker. Weights are random (seed 1802) unless stated
otherwise, inputs are synthetic, and dropout and stochastic depth are disabled, because both make even the stock program
non-reproducible.
A.2
Compiled-program experiments
What is measured.
For training we compile a function that runs the forward pass and an MSE loss against a fixed
random target, and then call backward(). There is no optimizer step. For inference we compile the model in evaluation
mode and run it under torch.no grad(). The stock baseline is Inductor with reorder for peak memory and
inplace buffers enabled, which is the default; only the FX-graph cache is disabled, so that every run compiles afresh.
The peak is the largest value of the profiler’s tracked tensor-allocation counter during one warm step. It includes the step’s
outputs, its loss and all gradients, and excludes the resident weights and inputs. The column “including the frame” of Table 4
adds the bytes of the parameters, buffers, inputs and target back to the denominator.
Protocol per configuration.
Each configuration runs in a fresh process and goes through the following steps.
1. Compile once with the stock compiler and check the compiled outputs and gradients against eager execution (rtol = 10−4,
atol = 10−5).
2. Run two warm steps, then one observed step in which every wrapper statement executes inside a profiler scope and the
storages bound to its assigned names are recorded.
3. Build the root model of every wrapper, compute the trap bounds (20 s limit each) and search for an order (60 s limit).
4. Install three versions of every wrapper in the same compiled module: the stock body, the stock unit order re-emitted by
our emitter (“normalized”), and the optimized order.
5. Measure the three versions twice each, alternating, and compare their outputs, losses and gradients bitwise.
6. Force the optimized order into Inductor’s reordering pass, recompile, and measure the regenerated program (“Regen.”).
The prediction error of a wrapper is the measured peak inside the wrapper’s window minus the predicted one. The prediction
is the stock entry level plus the model’s peak minus the model’s initial live bytes.
Configurations.
Transformer encoders and encoder–decoders are torch.nn modules with four heads and a feed-forward
width of four times the model width unless stated otherwise. Hugging Face models use their default configurations with the
stated numbers of layers. For BERT, DistilBERT, GPT-2, T5 and ViT these are the base or small sizes; the Llama models are
scaled down with hidden sizes 512 and 768. Vision models are torchvision definitions. The labels in the tables give the
batch size b, the sequence length s, the model width d and the number of layers.
Latency.
Each latency configuration alternates the stock and the reordered program over four rounds. Every round runs
three warm-up steps and then 5 to 50 timed steps per variant, depending on the model’s size. We report the ratio of the
medians.


--- Page 14 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
A.3
Operator-level inference experiments
For the microcontroller-class models (Section 5.2), the speaker-embedding networks (Section 5.3) and the YOLO detectors
we trace the model at the operator level and build an operator graph the way an embedded runtime sees it.
• Tracing. Small convolutional models are traced symbolically, with batch normalization folded into convolutions. The
others are traced with make fx on concrete shapes after functionalization, decomposing to core ATen operators but
keeping activations as single operators.
• Fusion. Elementwise operators with a single tensor input and the same number of elements (activations, decomposed
normalization) are fused into their producer when they are its only user.
• Views. View operators alias their source and own no buffer.
• Sizes. Activations are int8 for the microcontroller models and fp32 for the speaker and detection models; each surviving
operator owns one output buffer.
• Outputs. The model outputs are pinned until the end, so multi-output detectors are modeled correctly.
A schedule is executed operator by operator in Python, keeping exactly the values the schedule keeps. The executed peak
and the bitwise equality of all outputs with an unscheduled reference run are checked for every schedule we report. The
arena is computed with a TFLite-Micro-style greedy planner, which places buffers by decreasing size at the lowest offset
that does not conflict, with 16- or 64-byte alignment. MACs are counted with PyTorch’s FLOP counter.
A.4
Selective recomputation
Candidates for recomputation are values that are produced before the peak event of the current optimal order and have a
consumer after it. For each candidate we enumerate single anchors a among its ancestors whose cone, i.e. the operators
between a and the candidate, is closed: every input of an operator in the cone is a or lies in the cone. We keep the anchor
that saves the most bytes, preferring cheaper cones on ties. A transformation duplicates the cone, either once for all late
consumers or once per late consumer, and rewires those consumers to the copy. Every transformed graph is scheduled
exactly and certified with the trap bounds. A greedy loop applies the transformation with the lowest resulting peak as long
as the peak decreases and the extra MACs stay within the budget.
A.5
Theory experiments
The random DAG families of Section B.7 have between 8 and 15 vertices with integer weights between 1 and 8.
• random: edges with probability 0.15–0.45 to every earlier vertex;
• sp: random two-terminal series–parallel graphs;
• pumpkin: two to four chains between a source and a sink;
• intree: random in-trees;
• training: a forward chain followed by a backward chain that reads the saved forward activations.
Exact optima are computed by dynamic programming over all ideals. The capped experiments use exact Dijkstra search
over (live set, counters) states with uniform cap two.

gradients.
B.2

identical outputs. DeepLabV3 is the only configuration where the stock order is not optimal. RegNetY-400MF is the only
configuration where the bounds leave a gap: the order found there equals the stock order, and the bound is 13% below it.

B.4
Microcontroller-class models
Table 7 lists the 16 models of Section 5.2. In every model the order in which TFLite Micro executes the operators is certified
optimal, and the peak equals the inputs plus the output of a single operator.
B.5
Speaker-embedding networks and detectors
Table 8 completes Table 1 with the 0.8 s inputs and the greedy arena. For B3 and B6 the greedy planner does not realize the
saving, because of fragmentation. Table 9 reports the YOLO detectors at 640 × 640. In YOLOv5nu and YOLOv8n the peak
is the input image plus the output of the first convolution. In the other models it is a concatenation in the feature pyramid,
whose large inputs are both needed at the peak event. Selective recomputation therefore has almost nothing to work with,
which illustrates the condition stated in Section 5.3.
B.6
Negative rule families for gradient scheduling
A natural question is whether the savings of Section 5.4 follow a simple rule. Two candidate rules are “finish a stage’s
parameter-gradient branch before advancing the backbone” and “always defer parameter gradients”. Both can nearly double
the peak. Let a source produce a private activation a of size A and a tensor u of size 1. Operation G consumes a and u
and creates a pinned gradient of size P. Operation X consumes u and creates z of size 1 with scratch Q. Counting outputs
allocated before inputs are released, the two orders have peaks
peak(GX) = max(A + 1 + P, P + Q + 2),
peak(XG) = max(A + Q + 2, A + P + 2).
With A = 1 and P = Q = M, finishing G first costs 2M + 2, while deferring it costs M + 3. With A = Q = M and
P = 1 the outcomes are exchanged. Hence neither rule is safe; each loses a factor approaching two on one of the families.
B.7
Theory experiments
Table 10 breaks the comparison of the lower bounds with exact optima down by family. The reverse bound is exact on every
in-tree and training-shaped instance, which matches Theorem 6. Table 11 reports the number of states that our prototype of
the bounded-treewidth algorithm generates. The growth with K and B is the parameter dependence of Theorem 5, and it
confirms that the algorithm is a tractability statement rather than a practical tool.

Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
C
EXACT REALIZATION
C.1
The contract
The contract of Theorem 1 describes what a generated program must guarantee for a permutation of its statements to be both
correct and exactly predictable. Its state Q = (E, G, O, U, H) consists of five parts:
• the live storage epochs E, where an epoch is one allocation-to-free interval of a storage;
• the defined content generations G of byte regions inside those epochs;
• the owners O of each epoch, namely wrapper names, tuple slots, saved values, native references and returned values;
• the outstanding asynchronous uses U;
• any externally visible state H, such as random-number generators.
The six conditions are the following.
(C1) Every unit’s reads and writes are described at the level of byte regions and content generations, including partial writes
through aliases.
(C2) Every owner is recorded, and every access has completed before the storage it touches is released.
(C3) Every unit computes a deterministic function of the contents it reads.
(C4) The sequence of charged allocation and release events of every unit is the recorded one.
(C5) This sequence is independent of the surrounding live memory: executing a unit next to any disjoint live frame R adds
exactly |R| to every event and leaves R untouched.
(C6) Emitting a new order introduces no events other than those of the units, their allocations and their releases.
An order is admissible if it respects every conflicting pair of region accesses and every recorded ownership constraint.
C.2
Proof of Theorem 1
The proof has two parts, one about values and one about memory.
For values, consider two adjacent units in the reference order that have no conflicting accesses. Swapping them changes
neither the contents either of them reads nor the contents left behind, because their written regions are disjoint from each
other’s read and written regions. An admissible order can be reached from the reference order by such swaps. By (C1) and
(C3), every unit therefore reads, in the new order, exactly the content generations it read in the reference order and computes
the same result. If the units are deterministic at the byte level the results are bitwise equal.
For memory, we maintain a correspondence between the abstract state of the root model and the concrete state of the
program, event by event. Allocation creates a fresh epoch on both sides. Binding a name or saving a value adds the same
owner on both sides. Releasing a name removes it on both sides. A storage is freed only when its owner set is empty and its
accesses are complete, which happens at the same event on both sides by (C2). By (C4) the charged sizes match, and by
(C5) the bytes held by units that are not currently executing contribute the same constant to every event. By (C6) no other
events occur. Hence the live bytes agree after every event, and so do their maxima.
C.3
What breaks without each condition
Each condition is needed; the following small programs violate one condition each.
• Owner-sensitive call (C2). A root of size 10 has two owners, a and z. Unit D drops z. Unit K reads the root, drops a
and allocates an output of size 6. The order D, K peaks at 10, while K, D peaks at 16, with identical code and inputs.
• Hidden runtime state (C3, C5). A unit uses scratch 4 or 64 depending on a flag that another unit sets.
• Partial write through an alias (C1). One unit reads element zero through one view, another overwrites only element
zero through another view. Swapping them changes the returned value from 2 to 9.
• Asynchronous completion (C2). An asynchronous read observes a later overwrite unless completion is ordered before
the write.
• Regrouping (C6). Two units that each allocate and free 8 bytes peak at 8 when executed atomically and at 16 when their
events are interleaved.
• Envelope versus workspace. A unit that frees an input of 10 and then allocates an output of 6 has net change −4 and
maximal prefix change 0, so the commonly used difference between the two is 4 although the unit has no workspace.
• A late alias (observed during development). Emitting an alias only at the return statement kept a tuple, and with it a


--- Page 20 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
gradient, alive and raised the ResNet-18 backward peak by 16 KiB. Emitting aliases as early as their dependencies allow
restores exactness.
• The caching allocator (C5). On the GPU the block assigned to a request depends on the history of the allocator’s pools
(Section 5.6), which is the failure we measure there.
D
TRAP BOUNDS
Throughout, L(X) is the live memory after the ideal X, c(v) the event cost of v beyond the live memory, A(v) the strict
ancestors and D(v) the descendants of v including v.
D.1
Soundness and domination
Soundness of F.
Fix a proper ideal R and an arbitrary topological order. Let v be the first operation of the order outside
R. All ancestors of v precede it and lie in R, so v is in the ready frontier F(R). The set X of operations before v satisfies
A(v) ⊆X ⊆R, so the event of v costs L(X) + c(v) ≥fv(R) ≥minu∈F (R) fu(R). Taking the maximum over R gives
F ≤OPT.
Soundness of R.
Fix a nonempty ideal T and let v be the last operation of T in the order. Then v is maximal in T, and the
set of operations before v contains T \ {v} and contains no descendant of v. The event of v therefore costs at least qv(T).
Domination of G.
For every v the set Rv = V \ D(v) is an ideal whose ready frontier is exactly {v}. The ideals X with
A(v) ⊆X ⊆Rv are exactly the ideals that contain A(v) and exclude v. Hence fv(Rv) equals the event-cut term gv, and
F ≥maxv gv = G. Symmetrically, T = A(v) ∪{v} has the unique maximal element v and the interval [A(v), V \ D(v)],
so R ≥G.
D.2
Computation
At a capacity λ, call a ready operation v admissible for R if fv(R) ≤λ. Enlarging R can only enlarge the interval over
which fv minimizes, so admissibility persists. Saturating admissions from R = ∅therefore reaches a unique fixed point. If
the fixed point is a proper ideal R, every operation of its frontier has fv(R) > λ, which certifies F > λ. Conversely, if
some proper ideal T has minv∈F (T ) fv(T) > λ, no admission sequence can leave T. The first operation to leave it would
be admissible for an ideal contained in T, and hence for T itself, a contradiction. Saturation thus completes if and only
if λ ≥F. The adaptive algorithm avoids a search over λ: it admits an operation of minimum fv(R) at every step and
returns the largest value it recorded. It performs n admissions with at most n frontier evaluations each. Each evaluation is a
minimum-weight closure: operations carry their allocations, a release node per root carries a gain equal to the root’s size,
and infinite arcs encode precedence and the interval endpoints. This gives O(n2) minimum-cut computations. The reverse
bound removes maximal operations from V in the same way; its converse argument uses the first removed member of any
nonempty ideal.
D.3
Incomparability
• R > F. On the backward wrapper of DistilBERT (b1, s128) the forward bound is 266,237,960 B, while the reverse bound
and the optimum are both 266,628,104 B.
• F > R. Let two independent operations each consume their own external input of size 2 and use scratch 1, with initial
memory 4. Whichever runs first costs 5, so F = OPT = 5. In the reverse bound each operation may assume that the
other has already run, so R = 3, and 4 with the boundary terms.
D.4
Two families
Proposition 6. Let Th be a complete binary in-tree of height h ≥1 with unit weights, a zero-weight source feeding every
leaf, and a pinned root. Then F = 3 and R = OPT = h + 2.
Proof. OPT = h + 2. Evaluating one child subtree, keeping its root, then evaluating the other and finally the parent gives
h + 2 by induction. For the lower bound, restrict any order to each child subtree; by induction each restriction contains an
event with at least h + 1 live values. At the later of these two events the other subtree has already started and its parent has


--- Page 21 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
not yet run, so the other subtree holds at least one live value, which gives h + 2.
F = 3. Every internal vertex is admissible at capacity 3 using the ideal of its own ancestors, in which exactly its two
children are live. Hence saturation completes at capacity 3. The lowest internal vertex shows F ≥G ≥3.
R ≥h + 2. Let T consist of the source and all vertices of height at most one; its maximal elements are the vertices of
height one. Fix such a vertex v and an ideal X with T \ {v} ⊆X ⊆V \ D(v); here D(v) consists of v and its h −1 strict
ancestors. Both children of v lie in X and are live because v /∈X. For each strict ancestor a of v, let a′ be its child off the
path to v. The subtree of a′ meets X, because it contains vertices of height at most one. The restriction of X to that subtree
is a nonempty ideal of an in-tree whose root’s consumer a is not in X, so some maximal element of the restriction has an
unexecuted consumer and is live. These h −1 subtrees are disjoint from each other and from the children of v. Hence
L(X) ≥2 + (h −1) and qv(T) ≥h + 2, and soundness gives R ≤OPT.
Proposition 7. Let a zero-weight source feed k ≥2 unit-weight values a1, . . . , ak. Let a zero-weight merge mij consume
ai and aj for every pair i < j, and let a zero-weight sink consume all merges. Then F = 2 and R = OPT = k.
Proof. Computing all ai first and then all merges has peak k, so OPT ≤k. For F ≤2, consider a proper ideal R. If
some ai /∈R, it is ready with prefix {s} and costs 1. If all ai ∈R but some merge mij is not, its prefix {s, ai, aj} has
two live values. Otherwise only the sink is outside R and costs nothing. Every merge shows G ≥2. For R ≥k, let
T = {s, a1, . . . , ak}, whose maximal elements are the ai, and let X satisfy T \{ai} ⊆X ⊆V \D(ai). Every al with l̸ = i
lies in X, and its consumer mil lies in D(ai) and hence outside X, so al is live. Therefore qai(T) ≥1 + (k −1) = k.
Exhaustive computation confirms R = OPT also with merges of weight one for k ≤6, where F =
␀k

and R = OPT =
␀k
2

+ 2. Whether OPT/ max(F, R) is bounded on all DAGs remains open; the largest ratio we found is 1.5.
E
NECESSARY RECOMPUTATION
Lemma 8 (Projection). Let P ⊆V and let ZP be the one-shot instance with the weights of all vertices outside P set to zero
and the dependencies unchanged. If a capped schedule computes every vertex of P exactly once with peak at most B, then
OPT1(ZP ) ≤B.
Proof. The order of first computations is a topological order of ZP . A value of P that is computed only once cannot be
deleted while it is still needed, since it could not be recreated. It is therefore resident at every event of ZP at which the
one-shot schedule keeps it, and each one-shot event costs no more than the corresponding capped event.
The cover bound.
For an event h let ℓ(h) = wh + P
p∈pred(h) wp be its local footprint. Let Xh be the values produced by
strict ancestors of h that have a consumer among the strict descendants of h, excluding the inputs of h. Every value in Xh
that is computed only once must be resident at the first execution of h. With zv = 1[Nv ≥2] this gives the knapsack-cover
constraint
P
v∈Xh wvzv ≥ℓ(h) + P
v∈Xh wv −B.
Its fractional minimum of P
v cvzv, obtained greedily by increasing cv/wv, is a lower bound on the extra work. The
maximum over all events is the cover bound evaluated in Section 6. The constraints of all events can also be combined in
one covering linear program; a rational dual solution then certifies the bound without trusting the solver.
F
HARDNESS
F.1
Proof of Theorem 4
Membership.
With a uniform cap k, a normalized schedule has at most kn computations and at most kn deletions, so it is
a polynomial certificate whose peak can be checked in polynomial time.
Hardness.
We reduce from weighted one-shot pebbling on pumpkin graphs, which is strongly NP-hard (Jin et al., 2023).
Let (G, B) be an instance with sink t. First, make all weights positive: replace every weight wv by (n + 1)wv + 1 and B by
(n + 1)B + n. At most n values coexist, so this preserves the answer, and the numbers remain polynomial in unary. Next,
append the following gadget:


--- Page 22 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
• zero-weight vertices r1, . . . , rk and z1, . . . , zk−1, and barrier vertices h1, . . . , hk−1 of weight B;
• edges t →ri for every i, and ri →hi →zi →ri+1 for i < k;
• the new sink is rk, and every vertex receives the cap k.
If. Run a one-shot schedule of G with peak at most B, compute r1, delete every old value, compute h1 and z1, delete h1,
and repeat. Each phase stays within B, and every vertex is computed at most k times.
Only if. At the first computation of each barrier hi, no old value can be resident, because all old weights are positive and hi
alone has weight B. The first computation of ri+1 requires a fresh t, and hence a computation of every old vertex, after that
barrier, and the first r1 requires one before the first barrier. These k phases are disjoint, so with cap k every old vertex is
computed exactly once in each phase. Restricting any one phase to the old events yields a one-shot schedule of G with peak
at most B.
Treewidth. A pumpkin has treewidth two. Attach to a bag containing t the chain of bags {t, ri, hi}, {t, hi, zi}, {t, zi, ri+1}
for i = 1, . . . , k −1. These bags cover all new edges, every vertex occurs in a connected set of bags, and no bag has more
than three vertices.
F.2
Binary caps
If two moments of an execution have the same live set, the actions between them can be removed: the remaining schedule is
still valid, its counters only decrease and its peak does not increase. Hence caps above 2n are never needed, and with caps
written in binary the problem embeds unrestricted black pebbling, which is PSPACE-complete (Gilbert et al., 1980; Chan
et al., 2023).
F.3
Series–parallel graphs
The fork/join region.
Given items i with weights wi and prices ci, build a binary tree of zero-weight forks fI and joins
jI of weight W = C + 1, whose leaves are the item vertices ai of weight wi and price ci. The region is two-terminal
series–parallel with out-degree two. All of its values fit in B = P
i wi + (n −1)W.
Knapsack equality for minimum work with uniform cap two.
Append t →r1 →H →z →r2 and t →r2, where H
has weight B −C and the other new vertices have weight zero. At the first computation of H no join fits beside it, so the
resident item vertices form a set S with P
i∈S wi ≤C. After H, every join and every item outside S must be computed
again to produce t for r2. Conversely, every set S with P
S wi ≤C can be realized this way. Hence the minimum extra
work equals P
i ci −max{P
i∈S ci : P
i∈S wi ≤C}.
Partition with caps at most three.
Require three results of the region, separated by two barriers of weight B −C. Give
item vertices cap two and all other vertices cap three. An item that is absent at both barriers would need three computations,
so the item sets S1, S2 resident at the two barriers cover all items. Each has weight at most C, and the total weight is 2C, so
they form an exact partition.
An exponential trade-off frontier.
Take the path s →u1 →· · · →um →g →h →q →vm →· · · →v1 with
the additional edges ui →vi. Let w(ui) = c(ui) = ai = 2i−1, w(h) = H ≥A = P
i ai, and give all other vertices
weight and price zero. Keeping a subset S of the ui resident through h and recomputing the others realizes the pair
(M, E) = (H + a(S), A −a(S)) of peak and extra work. Every schedule satisfies M + E ≥H + A, so all 2m pairs are
non-dominated.
G
THE BOUNDED-TREEWIDTH ALGORITHM
G.1
Why the obvious interface fails
Take vertices s, u, a, h, c, t with weights 0, 10, 1, 100, 1, 1, edges s →u →a →h →c →t and u →t, and cap two
everywhere. In history A every vertex is computed once and u is kept through h, with peak 111. In history B u is discarded
before h and recomputed afterwards, with peak 101. Both end with the same resident boundary values and the same
boundary counters, yet history B has used up both computations of u. A later reset of weight 111 that requires the region
again can be completed after history A but not after history B. Hence resident boundary values and boundary counters do
not form a sufficient interface, even when no internal value is resident.


--- Page 23 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
G.2
Local witnesses and types
Fix a nice tree decomposition of width t, let h = t + 1, and let Xx, Vx and Ix = Vx \ Xx be the bag, the vertices below
node x and its private vertices. A local witness at x is a complete event sequence over Vx that starts and ends empty. It
computes every private vertex between one and its cap times, respects every edge inside Vx, and stays within B. Its boundary
word is the subsequence of compute and delete events of bag vertices, of length at most 2Kh. Between consecutive
boundary events, and before the first and after the last, we record the sequence of private resident weights and reduce it to its
typical sequence (Bodlaender et al., 2020), which has length at most 2B + 1. The type of a witness is its boundary word
together with these reduced profiles; the number of types is at most W(h, K) T (B)2Kh+1 with W ≤P
ℓ≤2Kh(2h)ℓand
T (B) = (B + 1)2B+1. For each type the algorithm retains an actual witness of minimum private work.
G.3
The invariant
The algorithm maintains word-preserving segmentwise one-way coverage: for every admissible local witness there is a
retained witness with the same boundary word, no more private work, and a private profile that stutter-dominates the other
one in every segment. Two facts make this invariant compose. First, typical sequences are compatible with concatenation
and with constant shifts, and they admit a merge lemma for sums of independent profiles (Bodlaender et al., 2020). Second,
private vertices interact with the rest of the schedule only through memory, and their caps have already been checked on the
retained witness. Replacing a witness by a retained one with the same word therefore keeps every surrounding schedule
valid without increasing its peak or its work. Typical equivalence is used only to deduplicate; the induction relies on one-way
domination.
G.4
Transitions
• Leaf. The empty witness.
• Introduce v. No private vertex is adjacent to v, so only edges inside the bag need checking. For every retained child
witness, a dynamic program over the position in that literal witness and the type of the prefix built so far inserts up to kv
compute/delete pairs of v. Equal prefix types at the same position have the same future, so one representative suffices; this
needs O(Kn) positions times a parameter-bounded number of types, not nK placements.
• Forget v. Relabel the events of v as private, which concatenates segments and shifts their levels by wv where v is resident,
require that v was computed at least once, and charge cv times its number of computations.
• Join. Combine two retained witnesses with identical boundary words: synchronize the bag events, interleave the private
events of the two children by a dynamic program over pairs of positions and the merged prefix type, count resident bag
values once, and add the private work.
• Root. At the empty root every vertex is private, so the retained witness is a complete schedule; truncating it after the first
computation of the sink gives the answer.
Every step uses polynomially many literal positions times a number of types that depends only on t, K and B, which gives
the bound f(t, K, B) poly(n, L) of Theorem 5.
G.5
Comparison-restricted augmentation
Let OPT(B, p) be the least work over schedules that never have more than p resident values of positive weight at an
allocation event. For 0 < ε ≤1 round every positive weight to ⌈wv/δ⌉with δ = εB/p, and solve exactly with budget
B′ = ⌊p/ε⌋+ p. Every comparison schedule fits in B′, because rounding adds at most p units at each event. The returned
schedule respects all caps, its true peak is at most δB′ ≤(1 + ε)B, and its work is at most OPT(B, p). The running time is
f(t, K, p, 1/ε) poly(n, L).
H
SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL
The supplementary archive reproduces every number, table and figure that concerns public models, and it contains all result
files behind them.
• experiments/harness/: fixed-wrapper realization for Inductor: wrapper capture, root models, emission, regenera-
tion and the per-configuration driver.
• experiments/edge/: operator-level graphs, schedule execution, the arena planner and selective recomputation.


--- Page 24 ---
Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust
• experiments/*.py: the study drivers, the CP-SAT baseline, the allocator simulation, and the scripts that regenerate
all tables and figures from the saved results.
• experiments/runs*/, edge/results/, edge/rdnpub/, theory/: the saved results.
• solvers/: the exact capacity search, the forward and reverse trap bounds, their independent verifiers, the CP-SAT
model with recomputation caps, and the prototype of the bounded-treewidth algorithm.
The README.md maps every section, table and figure to the command that produces it. The certificate verifiers and the
table scripts use only the Python standard library.
